ψεύσασθαι μὲν οὖν οὐ καθῆκόν ἐστι περὶ τῶν ἀναγραφομένων· εἰ δὲ καί τι παραβαίην, οὐχ ὅσιον ἐν τούτοις· ἀλλ᾽, ὡς γέγονεν, οὕτως διασαφοῦμεν ἀφοσιούμενοι πᾶν ἁμάρτημα. διόπερ ἐπειράθην ἀποδεξάμενος αὐτῶν τὴν τοῦ λόγου δύναμιν παρὰ τῶν ἀναγραφομένων ἕκαστα τῶν γινομένων ἔν τε τοῖς χρηματισμοῖς τοῦ βασιλέως καὶ ταῖς συμποσίαις μεταλαβεῖν.
ἔθος γάρ ἐστι, καθὼς καὶ σὺ γινώσκεις, ἀφ᾽ ἧς ἂν [ἡμέρας] ὁ βασιλεὺς ἄρξηται χρηματίζειν, μέχρις οὗ κατακοιμηθῇ, πάντα ἀναγράφεσθαι τὰ λεγόμενα καὶ πρασσόμενα, καλῶς γινομένου καὶ συμφερόντως.
τῇ γὰρ ἐπιούσῃ τὰ τῇ πρότερον πεπραγμένα καὶ λελαλημένα πρὸ τοῦ χρηματισμοῦ παραναγινώσκεται, καί, εἴ τι μὴ δεόντως γέγονε, διορθώσεως τυγχάνει τὸ πεπραγμένον.
πάντ᾽ οὖν ἀκριβῶς {παρὰ τῶν} ἀναγεγραμμένων, ὡς ἐλέχθη, μεταλαβόντες κατακεχωρίκαμεν, εἰδότες ἣν ἔχεις φιλομάθειαν εἰς τὰ χρήσιμα.

Μετὰ δὲ τρεῖς ἡμέρας ὁ Δημήτριος παραλαβὼν αὐτούς, καὶ διελθὼν τὸ τῶν ἑπτὰ σταδίων ἀνάχωμα τῆς θαλάσσης πρὸς τὴν νῆσον, καὶ διαβὰς τὴν γέφυραν, καὶ προσελθὼν ὡς ἐπὶ τὰ βόρεια μέρη, συνέδριον ποιησάμενος εἰς κατεσκευασμένον οἶκον παρὰ τὴν ἠϊόνα, διαπρεπῶς ἔχοντα καὶ πολλῆς ἡσυχίας ἔφεδρον, παρεκάλει τοὺς ἄνδρας τὰ τῆς ἑρμηνείας ἐπιτελεῖν, παρόντων ὅσα πρὸς τὴν χρείαν ἔδει καλῶς.
οἱ δὲ ἐπετέλουν ἕκαστα σύμφωνα ποιοῦντες πρὸς ἑαυτοὺς ταῖς ἀντιβολαῖς· τὸ δὲ ἐκ τῆς συμφωνίας γινόμενον πρεπόντως ἀναγραφῆς οὕτως ἐτύγχανε παρὰ τοῦ Δημητρίου.
καὶ μέχρι μὲν ὥρας ἐνάτης τὰ τῆς συνεδρείας ἐγίνετο· μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα περὶ τὴν τοῦ σώματος θεραπείαν ἀπελύοντο γίνεσθαι, χορηγουμένων αὐτοῖς δαψιλῶς ὧν προῃροῦντο πάντων.

ἐκτὸς δὲ καὶ καθ᾽ ἡμέραν, ὅσα βασιλεῖ παρεσκευάζετο, καὶ τούτοις ὁ Δωρόθεος ἐπετέλει· προστεταγμένον γὰρ ἦν αὐτῷ διὰ τοῦ βασιλέως. ἅμα δὲ τῇ πρωΐᾳ παρεγίνοντο εἰς τὴν αὐλὴν καθ᾽ ἡμέραν, καὶ ποιησάμενοι τὸν ἀσπασμὸν τοῦ βασιλέως, ἀπελύοντο πρὸς τὸν ἑαυτῶν τόπον.
ὡς δὲ ἔθος ἐστὶ πᾶσι τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις, {ἀπονιψάμενοι} τῇ θαλάσσῃ τὰς χεῖρας, ὡς ἂν εὔξωνται πρὸς τὸν θεόν, ἐτρέποντο πρὸς τὴν ἀνάγνωσιν καὶ τὴν ἑκάστου διασάφησιν.

Ἐπηρώτησα δὲ καὶ τοῦτο Τίνος χάριν ἀπονιζόμενος τὰς χεῖρας τὸ τηνικαῦτα εὔχονται; διεσάφουν δέ, ὅτι μαρτύριόν ἐστι τοῦ μηδὲν εἰργάσθαι κακόν· πᾶσα γὰρ ἐνέργεια διὰ τῶν χειρῶν γίνεται· καλῶς καὶ ὁσίως μεταφέροντες ἐπὶ τὴν δικαιοσύνην καὶ τὴν ἀλήθειαν πάντα.

καθὼς δὲ προειρήκαμεν, οὕτως καθ᾽ ἑκάστην εἰς τὸν τόπον, ἔχοντα τερπνότητα διὰ τὴν ἠσυχίαν καὶ καταύγειαν, συναγόμενοι τὸ προκείμενον ἐπετέλουν. συνέτυχε δὲ οὕτως ἐν ἡμέραις ἑβδομήκοντα δυσὶ τελειωθῆναι τὰ τῆς μεταγραφῆς, οἱονεὶ κατὰ πρόθεσίν τινα τοῦ τοιούτου γεγενημένου.

Τελείωσιν δὲ ὅτε ἔλαβε, συναγαγὼν ὁ Δημήτριος τὸ πλῆθος τῶν Ἰουδαίων εἰς τὸν τόπον, οὗ καὶ τὰ τῆς ἑρμηνείας ἐτελέσθη, παρανέγνω πᾶσι, παρόντων καὶ τῶν διερμηνευσάντων, οἵτινες μεγάλης ἀποδοχῆς καὶ παρὰ τοῦ πλήθους ἔτυχον, ὡς ἂνμεγάλων ἀγαθῶν παραίτιοι γεγονότες.
ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ τὸν Δημήτριον ἀποδεξάμενοι παρεκάλεσαν μεταδοῦναι τοῖς ἡγουμένοις αὐτῶν, μεταγράψαντα τὸν πάντα νόμον.

καθὼς δὲ ἀνεγνώσθη τὰ τεύχη, στάντες οἱ ἱερεῖς καὶ τῶν ἑρμηνέων οἱ πρεσβύτεροι καὶ τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ πολιτεύματος οἵ τε ἡγούμενοι τοῦ πλήθους εἶπον Ἐπεὶ καλῶς καὶ ὁσίως διηρμήνευται καὶ κατὰ πᾶν ἠκριβωμένως, καλῶς ἔχον ἐστίν, ἵνα διαμείνῃ ταῦθ᾽ οὕτως ἔχοντα, καὶ μὴ γένηται μηδεμία διασκευή.

πάντων δ᾽ ἐπιφωνησάντων τοῖς εἰρημένοις, ἐκέλευσαν διαράσασθαι, καθὼς ἔθος αὐτοῖς ἐστιν, εἴ τις διασκευάσει προστιθεὶς ἢ μεταφέρων τι τὸ σύνολον τῶν γεγραμμένων ἢ ποιούμενος ἀφαίρεσιν, καλῶς τούτο πράσσοντες, ἵνα διὰ παντὸς ἀένναα καὶ μένοντα φυλάσσηται.

Προσφωνηθέντων δὲ καὶ τούτων τῷ βασιλεῖ μεγάλως ἐχάρη· τὴν γὰρ πρόθεσιν, ἣν εἴχεν, ἀσφαλῶς ἔδοξε τετελειῶσθαι. παρανεγνώσθη δὲ αὐτῷ καὶ πάντα, καὶ λίαν ἐξεθαύμασε τὴν τοῦ νομοθέτου διάνοιαν. καὶ πρὸς τὸν Δημήτριον εἶπε Πῶς τηλικούτων συντετελεσμένων οὐδεὶς ἐπεβάλετο τῶν ἱστορικῶν ἢ ποιητῶν ἐπιμνησθῆναι;
ἐκεῖνος δὲ ἔφη Διὰ τὸ σεμνὴν εἶναι τὴν νομοθεσίαν καὶ διὰ θεοῦ γεγονέναι· καὶ τῶν ἐπιβαλλομένων τινὲς ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ πληγέντες τῆς ἐπιβολῆς ἀπέστησαν.

καὶ γὰρ ἔφησεν ἀκηκοέναι Θεοπόμπου, διότι μέλλων τινὰ τῶν προηρμηνευμένων ἐπισφαλέστερον ἐκ τοῦ νόμου προσιστορεῖν ταραχὴν λάβοι τῆς διανοίας πλεῖον ἡμερῶν τριάκοντα· κατὰ δὲ τὴν ἄνεσιν ἐξιλάσκεσθαι τὸν θεόν, σαφὲς αὐτῷ γενέσθαι, τίνος χάριν τὸ συμβαῖνόν ἐστι.
δι᾽ ὀνείρου δὲ σημανθέντος, ὅτι τὰ θεῖα βούλεται περιεργασάμενος εἰς κοινοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἐκφέρειν, ἀποσχόμενον δὲ οὕτως ἀποκαταστῆναι.

καὶ παρὰ Θεοδέκτου δὲ τοῦ τῶν τραγῳδιῶν ποιητοῦ μετέλαβον ἐγώ, διότι παραφέρειν μέλλοντός τι τῶν ἀναγεγραμμένων ἐν τῇ βίβλῳ πρός τι δρᾶμα τὰς ὄψες ἀπεγλαυκώθη· καὶ λαβὼν ὑπόνοιαν, ὅτι διὰ τοῦτ᾽ αὐτῷ τὸ σύμπτωμα γέγονεν, ἐξιλασάμενος τὸν θεὸν ἐν πολλαῖς ἡμέραις ἀποκατέστη.
Μεταλαβὼν δὲ ὁ βασιλεύς, καθὼς προεῖπον, περὶ τούτων τὰ παρὰ τοῦ Δημητρίου, προσκυνήσας ἐκέλευσε μεγάλην ἐπιμέλειαν ποιεῖσθαι τῶν βιβλίων καὶ συντηρεῖν ἁγνῶς.

παρακαλέσας δὲ καὶ τοὺς ἑρμηνεῖς, ἵνα παραγίνωνται πυκνότερον πρὸς αὐτόν, ἐὰν ἀποκατασταθῶσιν εἰς τὴν Ἰουδαίων,—δίκαιον γὰρ εἶπε τὴν ἐκπομπὴν αὐτῶν γενέσθαι· παραγενηθέντες δέ, ὡς θέμις, ἕξειν αὐτοὺς φίλου·, καὶ {πολυωρία} τῆς μεγίστης τεύξεσθαι παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ.

τὰ δὲ πρὸς τὴν ἐκπομπὴν αὐτῶν ἐκέλευσεν ἑτοιμάζειν, μεγαλομερῶς τοῖς ἀνδράσι χρησάμενος. ἑκάστῳ γὰρ στολὰς ἔδωκε τῶν κρατίστων τρεῖς καὶ χρυσίου τάλαντα δύο καὶ κυλίκιον ταλάντου καὶ τρικλίνου πᾶσαν κατάστρωσιν.

ἔπεμψε δὲ καὶ τῷ Ἐλεαζάρῳ μετὰ τῆς ἐκπομπῆς αὐτῶν ἀργυρόποδας κλίνας δέκα καὶ τὰ ἀκόλουθα πάντα καὶ κυλίκιον ταλάντων τριάκοντα καὶ στολὰς δέκα καὶ πορφύραν καὶ στέφανον διαπρεπῆ καὶ βυσσίνων ὀθονίων ἱστοὺς ἑκατὸν καὶ φιάλας καὶ τρυβλία καὶ κρατῆρας χρυσοῦς δύο πρὸς ἀνάθεσιν.

ἔγραψε δὲ καὶ παρακαλῶν, ἵνα, ἐάν τινες τῶν ἀνδρῶν προαιρῶνται πρὸς αὐτὸν ἀνακομισθῆναι, μὴ κωλύσῃ, περὶ πολλοῦ ποιούμενος τοῖς πεπαιδευμένοις συνεῖναι, καὶ εἰς τοιούτους τὸν πλοῦτον κατατίθεσθαι δαψιλῶς, καὶ οὐκ εἰς μάταια.

Σὺ δέ, καθὼς ἐπηγγειλάμην, ἀπέχεις τὴν διήγησιν, ὦ Φιλόκρατες. τέρπειν γὰρ οἴομαί σε ταῦτα ἢ τὰ τῶν μυθολόγων βιβλία. νένευκας γὰρ πρὸς περιεργίαν τῶν δυναμένων ὠφελεῖν διάνοιαν, καὶ ἐν τούτοις τὸν πλείονα χρόνον διατελεῖς. πειράσομαι δὲ καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ τῶν ἀξιολόγων ἀναγράφειν, ἵνα διαπορευόμενος αὐτὰ κομίζῃ τοῦ βουλήματος τὸ κάλλιστον ἔπαθλον.

unit.reading: ARISTEAS TO PHILOCRATES

Since the narrative concerning our meeting with Eleazar, the high priest of the Jews, is worthy of note, Philocrates, and because you have set great store by hearing an account of the purpose and cause of our mission, reminding me at every opportunity, I have attempted to set it forth clearly for you, having recognized your love of learning,

which is the greatest thing for a human being—always to be learning something more and acquiring knowledge, either through historical accounts or through personal experience of the events themselves. For in this way a pure disposition of soul is formed, having taken up the noblest things; and having inclined toward that which is most sovereign of all, piety, it governs itself using an unerring rule.

Having set our purpose upon a meticulous examination of divine matters, we offered ourselves for an embassy to the aforementioned man, who is held in high esteem both by his fellow citizens and by others for his nobility of character and renown, and who possessed the greatest benefit for those with him and for the citizens in other places—namely, for the translation of the divine Law, because among them it is written on parchment scrolls in Hebrew characters.

This embassy we undertook with eagerness, having found an opportune moment with the king concerning those who had been relocated to Egypt from Judea by the king’s father, who had first gained possession of the city and taken over rule throughout Egypt. It is worthwhile to make these things known to you as well.

For I am convinced that you have an inclination rather toward the holiness and the disposition of those who conduct their lives according to the holy legislation—concerning which we have chosen {to inform you, and that you will gladly} listen, having recently arrived to us from the island and desiring to hear all that contributes to the edification of the soul.

Previously as well, I sent you a written record concerning the things I considered worthy of mention, which we received from the most learned high priests in most learned Egypt concerning the race of the Jews.

For since you are eager to learn about things that can benefit the intellect, it is proper to share them, especially with all like-minded people, but much more with you, who possess a genuine purpose—not only being a brother to me by kinship of character, but also being one with us in the striving after the good.

For the charm of gold or any other construction prized among the vain does not offer the same benefit as the cultivation of education and the care devoted to these things. But lest we prolong these introductory words and turn into babblers, we will return to the continuous narrative.

Demetrius of Phalerum, having been appointed over the king’s library, was granted large sums of money in order to collect, if possible, all the books throughout the inhabited world; and by making purchases and transcriptions he brought the king’s purpose to completion, as far as it depended on him.

Being asked, then, in our presence, "How many tens of thousands of books are there?" he said, "More than twenty, O king; but I will make effort in a short time to fill up the remainder to fifty tens of thousands. Moreover, it has been reported to me that the laws of the Jews are worthy of transcription and of a place in your library."

"What is there to prevent you from doing this?" he said. "For all the means necessary for the work are placed at your disposal." And Demetrius said, "It requires translation; for they use characters peculiar to the Jews, just as the Egyptians do in the arrangement of their letters, just as they also have their own language. They are supposed to use the Syrian language, but this is not the case; rather, it is another manner of speech." And having learned the particulars, the king ordered that a letter be written to the high priest of the Jews, so that the aforementioned matters might reach completion.

And considering it an opportune time regarding the matters about which I had often made request to Sosibius of Tarentum and Andreas, the captains of the royal bodyguard—concerning the ransom of those who had been transported from Judea by the king’s father (for he, having invaded all the regions of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia, taking advantage of good fortune combined with bravery, had relocated some and made captives of others, reducing everything to subjugation through fear; in the course of which he transported up to a hundred thousand people from the land of the Jews to Egypt,

of whom he armed about thirty thousand chosen men and settled them in the fortresses throughout the country—though even earlier a substantial number had entered with the Persian, and prior to these, other allied forces had been sent out to fight with Psammetichus against the king of the Ethiopians, yet they had not come in such great numbers as those whom Ptolemy the son of Lagus transported)—

and as we said before, having selected the best in age and those preeminent in strength, he armed them, but the remaining mass of older and younger men, and women besides, he allowed to be reduced to slavery, not so much having this intent in his own heart as being prevailed upon by the soldiers on account of the services they had rendered in military campaigns—we, having obtained an opportunity for their release, as previously indicated, addressed the king in words such as these:

"Let it not be that we are refuted by the facts themselves, O king. For since the legislation given to all the Jews is that which we intend not only to transcribe but also to translate, what reason will we have for our mission, while a considerable number of them remain in slavery in your kingdom? But with a perfect and generous soul release those who are held in distress, since the God who gave them the Law directs your kingdom, as I have investigated.

For they worship the God who oversees and created all things, whom all people also worship, though we, O king, address him differently as Zen and Zeus; and the ancients not inappropriately indicated that he through whom all things are given life and come to be is the ruler and lord of all. Therefore, having surpassed all humanity in the splendor of your soul, grant release to those held in servitude."

And without delaying long, while we prayed in our souls to God to prepare his mind so that all might be released (for the race of humankind, being a creation of God, is both transformed and turned again by him; wherefore in many and various ways I invoked the Lord of the heart, that he might be compelled to accomplish what I requested;

for I had great hope, when proposing a discourse concerning the salvation of human beings, that God would bring about the fulfillment of the requests; for what people intend to do in holiness for righteousness and the practice of good deeds, God the Lord of all directs their actions and enterprises),

he looked up and, gazing with a cheerful countenance, said, "How many tens of thousands do you suppose there will be?" And Andreas, who was standing by, declared, "A little more than a hundred thousand." And he said, "Aristeas asks a small thing of us indeed!" Then Sosibius and some of those present said, "For it is worthy of your magnanimity that you offer their release as a thank-offering to the greatest God. For having been honored to the highest degree by the one who holds all power and glorified above your ancestors, it is fitting for you to offer the greatest thank-offerings."

And being well pleased, he ordered that the amount be added to the soldiers' allowances, and that twenty drachmas be paid for each slave, and that a decree be issued concerning these matters, and that the registration be made immediately. Thus he acted with magnificent generosity, God having fulfilled our entire purpose and having compelled him to ransom not only those who had arrived with his father’s army, but also any who had been there before or were introduced into the kingdom afterwards. They showed that the expenditure was more than four hundred talents.

And I think it not useless that a copy of the decree has been recorded. For the king's munificence will be far more evident and clear, God strengthening him to become the means of salvation to vast numbers.

And it was as follows: "By order of the King: All those who campaigned with our father into the regions of Syria and Phoenicia and, having invaded the country of the Jews, gained possession of Jewish persons and brought them into the city and the country, or even sold them to others—likewise also if any such were there beforehand or have been introduced since—those holding them shall release them immediately, receiving at once twenty drachmas for each person: the soldiers by payment with their wages, and the rest from the royal treasury.

For we consider that they were taken captive both contrary to the will of our father and contrary to what is right, and that by military rashness their land was devastated and the relocation of the Jews to Egypt occurred. For the plunder obtained by the soldiers from the open country was sufficient; wherefore the subjugation of human beings is completely unjust.

Since, therefore, we acknowledge that justice must be rendered to all men, and much more to those who are unjustly oppressed, and since in every way we seek what is right with respect to justice and piety toward all, we have decreed that as many Jewish persons as are in servitude {anywhere} in any manner within the kingdom shall be released by those holding them upon receiving the stated sum, and that no one shall act maliciously in dealing with these matters; but the registrations shall be made within three days from the day on which the decree is published, before the officers appointed over these matters, immediately presenting the persons as well.

For we have determined that it is expedient both for us and for the realm that this be carried out. Anyone who wishes may inform against those who disobey, on condition that he shall obtain ownership of the person proved guilty; and the property of such persons shall be confiscated to the royal treasury."

When the decree was submitted to be read again to the king, containing all the other provisions except "and if any such were there beforehand or have been introduced since," the king himself added this, displaying munificence and magnanimity; and he ordered that the sum of money, being a large lump sum, be distributed to the paymasters of the regiments and the royal bankers.

Having been so resolved, it was ratified within seven days; and the expenditure amounted to more than six hundred and sixty talents. For many of the infants at the breast were also being freed along with their mothers. When the question was additionally raised whether twenty drachmas should be given for these as well, the king ordered this to be done too, carrying out in full every detail of what had been resolved.

When these things were accomplished, he commanded Demetrius to submit a report concerning the transcription of the Jewish books. For all matters were administered by these kings through decrees and with great precision, and nothing was done carelessly or at random. Therefore I have also recorded a copy of the memorial, and copies of the letters, and the quantity of the items sent, and the construction of each, because each of them was distinguished by munificence and artistry. And the copy of the memorial is as follows:

"To the Great King from Demetrius. In accordance with your command, O king, concerning the books lacking to complete the library, that they should be collected, and that those which have fallen into disrepair should receive appropriate restoration, having applied no casual care to these matters, I report to you as follows:

The books of the Law of the Jews, along with a few others, are missing. For they happen to be written in Hebrew characters and language, but they have been transcribed rather carelessly and not as they ought to be, as is reported by those who know; for they have not received royal care.

And it is necessary that these too should be available to you in an accurate form, because this legislation is both more philosophical and uncorrupted, being indeed divine. For this reason writers, poets, and the multitude of historians have kept far away from mentioning the aforementioned books and the men who lived [and are living] according to them, because the contemplation contained in them is pure and sacred, as Hecataeus of Abdera says.

If it seems good, therefore, O king, let a letter be written to the high priest in Jerusalem to send men of the finest life and advanced in years, who are experts in their own Law, six from each tribe, so that, having examined the agreement among the majority and having obtained accuracy in the translation, we may place it in a notable manner, worthily both of the subject matter and of your purpose. Farewell always."

When this memorial had been submitted, the king ordered that a letter be written to Eleazar concerning these things, indicating also the redemption of the captives that had taken place. And he also gave, for the manufacture of mixing bowls, libation bowls, a table, and cups for libations, fifty talents weight of gold, seventy talents of silver, and a substantial quantity of precious stones—commanding the treasurers to give the craftsmen their choice of whatever they might prefer—and about a hundred talents of coin for sacrifices and other expenses.
And we shall describe the manufacture to you when we have gone through the copies of the letters. Now the king’s letter was of the following type:

King Ptolemy to Eleazar the high priest, greetings and good health. Since it happens that many of the Jews have been settled in our country, having been uprooted from Jerusalem by the Persians during the period of their supremacy, and furthermore having come into Egypt as captives along with our father—

of whom he enrolled many into the military corps at higher rates of pay, and likewise, having judged those already present to be faithful, he built fortresses and assigned them to them, so that the Egyptian nation might not be held in fear on their account; and we too, having succeeded to the kingdom, deal more benevolently with all, and much more so with your fellow citizens—

we have freed more than one hundred thousand captives, paying their masters the appropriate monetary price, and setting right whatever was done amiss through the impulses of the mobs, having resolved to act piously in this, and dedicating a thank-offering to the greatest God, who has preserved our kingdom in peace and supreme glory throughout the whole inhabited world; and we have appointed those of prime age into the army, while those capable of being near our person and worthy of confidence at court we have placed in positions of responsibility.

And since we desire to show favor both to these and to all the Jews throughout the inhabited world and to those who come after, we have resolved that your Law be translated into Greek letters from what is called Hebrew script among you, so that these books also may be in our library along with the other royal books.

You will do well, therefore, and in a manner worthy of our zeal, to select elders of upright life, who possess experience in the Law and the ability to translate, six from each tribe, so that from the majority agreement may be found, since the investigation concerns matters of great importance. For we consider that when this is accomplished we shall achieve great glory.

We have sent regarding these matters Andreas of the chief bodyguards and Aristeas, who are honored among us, to confer with you and to bring first-fruits of dedicatory gifts for the temple and for sacrifices and other needs, one hundred talents of silver. And if you write to us concerning whatever you wish, it will be a gratification, and you will act worthily of friendship, since whatever you choose will be performed with the utmost speed. Farewell.

To this letter Eleazar replied appropriately as follows: Eleazar the high priest to King Ptolemy, genuine friend, greetings. If you yourself and Queen Arsinoe, your sister, and the children are in good health, it would be well and as we desire; we too are in good health.

Having received the letter from you, we rejoiced greatly because of your resolve and good purpose, and having assembled the whole multitude, we read it aloud to them, so that they might know the piety you have toward our God. We also exhibited the bowls which you sent, twenty of gold and thirty of silver, five craters, and a table for dedication, and for the offering of sacrifices and for repairs of whatever the temple may require, one hundred talents of silver,

which Andreas, one of those honored by you, and Aristeas brought, noble and virtuous men, distinguished in culture, and in every way worthy of your conduct and justice; who also communicated your message to us, in reply to which they also heard from us what is fitting for your letter.

For in everything that is advantageous to you, even if it be beyond nature, we will comply; for this is a mark of friendship and love. For you have conferred great and unforgettable benefits upon our fellow citizens in many ways.

Immediately, therefore, we offered sacrifices on behalf of you and your sister and your children and friends; and all the multitude prayed that it may be with you as you purpose at all times, and that God, the ruler of all, may preserve your kingdom in peace with glory, and that the transcription of the holy Law may turn out advantageously and safely for you.

And in the presence of all, we selected noble and good elders, six from each tribe, whom we also sent having the Law. You will do well, therefore, righteous king, to command that as soon as the transcription of the books is completed, the men may again be restored safely to us. Farewell.

And they are: of the first tribe, Joseph, Hezekiah, Zechariah, John, Hezekiah, Elisha; of the second, Judah, Simon, Samuel, Adaiah, Mattathias, Eschlemias; of the third, Nehemiah, Joseph, Theodosius, Baseas, Ornias, Dakis;
of the fourth, Jonathan, Abaios, Elisha, Hananiah, Chabrias, [Hilkiah?]; of the fifth, Isaac, Jacob, Jesus, Sabbataios, Simon, Levi; of the sixth, Judah, Joseph, Simon, Zechariah, Samuel, Shelemiah;

of the seventh, Sabbataios, Zedekiah, Jacob, Isaac, Jesias, Natthaios; of the eighth, Theodosius, Jason, Jesus, Theodotus, John, Jonathan; of the ninth, Theophilus, Abraham, Arsamos, Jason, Endemias, Daniel;

of the tenth, Jeremiah, Eleazar, Zechariah, Benaiah, Elisha, Dathaios; of the eleventh, Samuel, Joseph, Judah, Jonathan, Chabeu, Dositheus; of the twelfth, Isaelos, John, Theodosius, Arsamos, Abietes, Ezekiel. In all, seventy-two.

And such was the reply made to the king's letter by Eleazar and his colleagues. But as I promised to give an account of the craftsmanship, I will do so. For they were executed with exceptional artistic skill, since the king made a lavish contribution and oversaw the craftsmen at every step. Therefore, they could neglect nothing nor finish anything carelessly. First, then, I will describe to you the details concerning the table.

Now the king was eager to make the piece of furniture immense in its dimensions. He commanded inquiries to be made of those in the area as to how large the former one was that stood in the temple in Jerusalem.

When they stated the dimensions, he further asked whether he should make a larger one. Some of the priests and the others said that nothing prevented it. But he said that he wished to make it even five times larger in size, but doubted lest it might become useless for the sacred services.
For he did not choose that his gifts should merely lie in the place, but rather he would be much more pleased if those responsible properly performed the fitting services upon the things he had made.

For it was not from a lack of gold that the previously constructed items were of modest dimensions, but it appears, he said, that they were formed in this way according to some design. For had there been an instruction, nothing would have been lacking; wherefore one must not transgress nor exceed what is well established.

He therefore ordered that the greatest variety of artistry should be employed, having noble thoughts in all things and possessing an innate capacity to discern the aesthetic effect of things. Whatever was unprescribed by scripture he commanded to be made for beauty, but whatever was written down, to follow its measurements.

For they made its length two cubits and its height a cubit and a half, fashioning the work entirely of solid, tested gold—I mean not that gold was plated around something, but that the wrought plate itself was attached.

And they made a border a handbreadth wide all around; and the moldings were twisted, having the relief of ropework raised in relief, wondrously fashioned in its progression on all three sides; for it was triangular.

And on each side the design of the workmanship had the same arrangement, so that whichever way it might be turned, the appearance was the same; and as it rested upon the border, the slope toward the table itself possessed the design of beauty, while the outer slope faced the view of the one approaching.

Consequently, the crest of the two slopes was sharp, projecting upward, as we said before, formed as a triangle, whichever way it might be turned. And arrangements of precious stones were set in it between the ropework motifs; one alongside another, they had an interwoven pattern inimitable in workmanship.
And they were all secured through perforations by golden pins for safety. And at the corners, clasps locked them together for stability.

Along the sides around the border, toward the upper face, an egg-and-dart pattern set with stones had been crafted, having a prominent embossed relief with continuous fluted carvings, placed closely against one another all around the table.

And beneath the relief of the stones of the egg-and-dart pattern, the craftsmen made a wreath of all kinds of fruit, prominently displaying clusters of grapes and ears of grain, and also dates and apples, olives, pomegranates, and the like. And having fashioned the stones to represent the aforesaid fruits, possessing the color of each kind, they bound them with the gold all around the entire construction of the table at the brim.

And after the arrangement of the wreath, similarly in keeping with the design of the egg-and-dart pattern, the rest of the fluting and engraving was crafted, because the table was made for use on either side, whichever way they might lift it, so that the position of the moldings and the border was also near the part with the feet.

For they made a solid plate across the entire width of the table four fingers thick, so that the feet could be inserted into it, having pins with clasps fastened along the border, so that whichever side they might lift, it could be used; and this is seen on the surface, the construction being ambidextrous.

And upon the table itself they made a maeander pattern in relief, having precious stones of various kinds prominent in the center—rubies and emeralds, and also onyx and other kinds remarkable in beauty.

And after the arrangement of the maeander pattern there was applied an openwork weave, wondrously made, producing a rhomboid design in the center; upon it crystal and what is called amber were embossed, creating an inimitable sight for the beholders.
And they made the feet with lily-shaped capitals, lilies curving back under the table, while the petals on the inner face were upright.

And the base of the foot resting upon the ground was an anthrax stone a handbreadth in every dimension, having the order of a plinth in its appearance, and eight fingers in width, upon which the entire plate of the foot rested.

They also fashioned ivy shooting forth and intertwining with acanthus from the stone, winding around the leg on all sides along with grape clusters made of precious stones, reaching up to the top. The same design was on all four legs, everything expertly executed and attached, possessing such supreme skill and art in exact imitation of reality that whenever a breeze stirred in the air, the leaves appeared to move, since everything was modeled in accordance with natural appearance.

And they made the surface of the table tripartite, like a triptych, fitted together by dovetailed mortises through the thickness of the structure, making the joining of the seams unseen and undetectable. The thickness of the entire table was no less than half a cubit, so that the whole work required many talents.

For since the king had chosen not to add anything to the dimensions, he expended even more than what would have been spent had larger ones been made; and according to his purpose everything was completed marvelously and remarkably, matchless in craftsmanship and distinguished in beauty.
Of the mixing bowls, two were of gold in construction, having an embossed scale pattern running from the base up to the middle, with stones skillfully set between the scales.

Above this was a meander pattern a cubit high, whose relief was composed of stones of various colors, displaying the painstaking effort of the craftsmanship along with its loveliness. Over this was fluting, upon which was a pattern of intertwined lozenges, presenting a net-like appearance up to the rim.

In the spaces between, small medallions of various stones of alternating kinds, no less than four fingers wide, completed the striking beauty. Upon the rim of the body were figures of lilies with flower-clusters, and interwoven strings of vine-clusters were fashioned all around.

Such, then, was the construction of the golden bowls, holding more than two metretes; but the silver ones were smooth in their workmanship, having a mirror-like surface made wonderfully for this very purpose, so that whatever was brought near was reflected more clearly than in looking-glasses.

It is not possible to describe the effects produced to create such a lifelike impression. For when they were finished and the vessels were arranged side by side—that is, first a silver bowl, then a golden one, and again a silver and a golden one—the appearance of the display was completely indescribable, and those who came to view it were unable to turn away because of the dazzling brilliance and delight of the sight.

For the effect of the surface was multifaceted. When onlookers gazed at the golden work itself, there was a kind of enchanting wonder as the mind continuously turned to each artistic detail. And again, whenever someone wished to look toward the placement of the silver vessels, everything all around shone back to wherever one was standing, producing even greater delight for the viewers, so that the ingenious artistry of the workmanship was utterly beyond description.

They embossed the golden bowls with wreaths of grapevine around the middle, and around the rims they wove in relief a wreath of ivy, myrtle, and olive, setting precious stones into it; and they executed the remaining courses with variation, striving eagerly to accomplish everything for the preeminent glory of the king.
In general, there was no such craft in its lavishness and artistry either in the royal treasuries or anywhere else. For the king took no small care, having great ambition for fine craftsmanship.

For he often neglected public business and sat diligently beside the craftsmen so that they would complete the works in a manner fitting the place to which they were being sent. Therefore, everything was made majestically and worthily both of the king who sent them and of the high priest presiding over the place.

For the quantity of stones was lavish, and they were large in size, no fewer than five thousand; and all were superior in craftsmanship, so that the gift of stones and the labor of the arts were worth five times as much as the gold.

Supposing, therefore, that an account of these things is also necessary, I have set it forth for you. The following section contains our journey to Eleazar; but first I will describe the layout of the entire country. For when we arrived at the region, we beheld the city situated in the middle of the whole land of Judea upon a mountain rising to a great height.

Upon the summit the temple had been built magnificently; and there were three surrounding walls, more than seventy cubits in height, and the breadth and length corresponded to the layout of the house, with everything having been constructed with magnificent generosity and surpassing expenditure in every respect.
And from the doorway and the fastenings around it along the doorposts, as well as the stability of the lintels, the unsparing expenditure of money was evident.

The design of the curtain was entirely similar to a doorway; and especially because of the rush of the air, the fabric was in continuous motion, since the breeze coming up from the floor made the folds billow right up to the upper extension, providing a pleasant sight that was hard to look away from.

The construction of the altar was built in proportion to the place and to the victims consumed by the fire, and the incline of the ascent to it was appropriately suited to the decorum of the place for the officiating priests, who were covered down to the ankles in linen tunics.

The house faces east, and its back parts toward the west; and the entire pavement is paved with stone and has slopes toward the appropriate places for the purpose of the water supply that is used to wash away the blood from the sacrifices. For many tens of thousands of animals are offered on feast days.

There is an inexhaustible supply of water, as a copious natural spring flows from within, and there are also marvelous and indescribable reservoirs beneath the ground, extending—as they showed—for five stadia around the foundation of the temple, with countless pipes leading from each of them, the streams converging with one another at every part.

And all these were lined with lead on the bottom and the walls; and over these a great quantity of plaster had been poured, with everything having been constructed effectively. The openings at the base are numerous, invisible to all except those whose duty it is to perform the service, so that in an instant and at a signal all the massive accumulation of sacrificial blood is cleansed away.

Being personally convinced, I will also describe the construction of the reservoirs just as I was assured of it. For they led me more than four stadia outside the city, and at a certain place they told me to bend down and listen closely to the noise produced by the meeting of the waters, so that the vast size of the receptacles became clear to me, as has been described.

The ministry of the priests is unsurpassed in every respect, in physical strength and in the arrangement of order and silence. For all work voluntarily despite great hardship, and each attends to what is assigned to him. They minister without ceasing: some bring the wood, some the olive oil, some the fine flour, others the spices, while others offer the burnt offerings of flesh, exercising exceptional strength.

For taking the legs of the calves with both hands, each weighing almost more than two talents, they heave them with both hands to a considerable height in a marvelous manner, and they never miss their placement. In like manner, the parts of the sheep and also of the goats are remarkable in weight and fatness. For since those whose duty it is select in every case animals that are unblemished and preeminent in fatness, what was mentioned above is accomplished.
A place is set apart for them to rest, where those taking a rest sit down. When this happens, those who have rested rise up eagerly, without anyone directing their service.

A complete silence prevails, so that one would suppose not a single person was present in the place, although there are about seven hundred ministers present—and a great multitude of those bringing the sacrifices—yet everything is performed with awe and in a manner worthy of great divinity.

It caused us great astonishment when we saw Eleazar in his ministry, both for the vestments and the glory consisting in the wearing of the robe he puts on and the stones upon it; for golden bells are around his ankle-length robe, giving off a distinctive musical sound, and on either side of these are pomegranates embroidered with flowers, marvelous in color.

He was girded with an extraordinary, magnificent sash, woven with the most beautiful colors. Upon his chest he wears what is called the oracle, in which are set twelve stones differing in kind, mounted in gold, with the names of the tribal heads according to the original arrangement, each radiating an indescribable natural color of its own kind.

Upon his head he wears what is called the turban, and upon this the inimitable diadem, the consecrated royal crown bearing in relief on a golden plate in sacred letters the name of God, between the eyebrows, full of glory—he who has been judged worthy of these things in the services.

The combined appearance of these things produces awe and trembling, so that one thinks he has entered into another world outside of this one; and I affirm that any person coming to the sight of the things described will fall into astonishment and indescribable wonder, transformed in mind because of the holy construction of each part.

For in order to gain a full understanding of everything, we went up to the citadel adjacent to the city and observed; it is situated in a very high place, fortified with many towers built up to the summit with large stones, as we learned, for the defense of the places around the temple,

so that, if any assault or insurrection or enemy invasion should occur, no one could make an approach to the enclosures around the house; for catapults and various engines were set upon the towers of the citadel, and the place was poised above the aforesaid enclosures,

the towers being guarded, as it were, by the most faithful men who had given great proofs of devotion to their homeland; and they did not have permission to leave the citadel except on festivals, and then only in part, nor did they allow anyone to enter.

They maintained strict scrutiny even if an order came through the governor to admit anyone for viewing, as indeed happened in our case. For with difficulty they admitted the two of us, being unarmed, to observe the sacrifices.

And they said that this procedure was confirmed by oaths; for all of them, being five hundred in number, had sworn that they were under divine obligation to fulfill the requirement according to the regulation, and not to admit more than five persons at the same time; for the citadel is the whole safeguard of the temple, and its founder had thus secured the advance protection of the aforementioned places.

The size of the city is of moderate proportion, its circuit being about forty stadia, as far as one can conjecture. The arrangement of its towers is like a theater, with visible thoroughfares—some below and others above according to custom—and passages through them. For the lay of the land rises terrace-like, since the city is built on a mountain. There are also stairways leading to the thoroughfares.

For some make their way along the upper levels and others beneath them, keeping well separated from each other along the route on account of those undergoing purifications, so that they may touch nothing that is forbidden.

Not without reason did the first founders construct the city in proper proportion, but with wise design. For since the country is extensive and fair, partly flat—namely the region called Samaria and the parts bordering the territory of the Idumaeans—and partly mountainous, [there is need for constant devotion] to agriculture and cultivation of the land, so that for this reason they may have abundant crops; and as this takes place, everything is cultivated with great abundance throughout all the aforementioned country.

Now in the case of all cities that possess great size and consequent prosperity, it happens that they are populous while the countryside is neglected, since everyone tends toward self-indulgent amusement and all people are naturally prone to pleasures.

This used to happen in Alexandria, which surpasses all cities in size and prosperity; for those who migrated to it from the country stayed on for a long time and brought about a decline in agricultural labor.

Therefore the king, so that they might not settle permanently, ordered that they should not stay for more than twenty days; and likewise he gave written instructions to the administrative officials that, if it were necessary to summon someone, they should settle the matter within five days.

Attaching great importance to this, he also appointed royal judges and their subordinate officers in every district, so that the farmers and their advocates in the city might not, by seeking profit, diminish the stores—that is, the produce of agriculture.

We have made this digression because Eleazar had so clearly explained these aforementioned matters to us. For great is the industry of the farmers. Indeed, their land is thickly planted with olive groves and rich in grain crops and legumes, as well as vines and abundant honey; as for other fruit trees and date palms, they cannot even be counted among them.

There are also many cattle of all kinds, and pasture for them is bountiful. Therefore they rightly perceived that the regions require a large population, and they proportioned the layout of the city and the villages accordingly.

A great abundance of spices, precious stones, and gold is also brought into the place by way of the Arabs. For the country is productive and well adapted for trade, the city is skilled in many crafts, and it lacks none of the goods brought across the sea.

For it has commodious harbors that supply it, namely at Ascalon, Joppa, and Gaza, as well as Ptolemais, which was founded by the king. It lies centrally in relation to the aforementioned places, not being far from them. The country has everything in abundance, being well-watered on every side and possessing great security.

The river called the Jordan flows around it, ever-flowing. Although the land anciently consisted of not less than sixty million arourae (though later the neighboring peoples encroached upon it), six hundred thousand men were established as landholders, each possessing a hundred arourae. When the river overflows, like the Nile, in the days near harvest time, it irrigates a large part of the land.

It empties its current into another river in the region of the Ptolemaeans, and this one flows out into the sea. Other streams, called winter-torrents, flow down, encompassing the regions toward Gaza and the territory of Azotus.

The country is enclosed by natural defenses, being difficult to invade and impassable for large forces, because the passes are narrow, with adjacent precipices and deep ravines, and the entire mountainous area surrounding the whole country is rugged.

It was also said that copper and iron mines formerly operated in the adjacent mountains of Arabia. But these fell into disuse at the time when the Persians held sway, since the governors of that time spread a false report that the mining was unprofitable and extremely expensive,

in order that the land might not be ruined through the mining of these metals, and almost alienated under Persian domination, since they would find a pretext for entering the territory because of this false report. As much as was necessary concerning these matters, then, I have indicated to you in summary, brother Philocrates; and I will explain next what relates to the translation.

For Eleazar selected the best men and those preeminent in learning, as having been born of distinguished parents, men who had not only acquired mastery of Jewish literature, but had also given no casual attention to the culture of the Greeks.

For this reason they were also well-suited for embassies, and they performed this duty whenever necessary; and they possessed great aptitude for discussions and inquiries concerning the Law, having cultivated the middle course of character (for this is most noble), having laid aside any rough and uncouth disposition of mind, and likewise having overcome conceit and thinking themselves superior to others. Instead, they embraced conversation, listening attentively and replying appropriately to every matter, all of them maintaining these qualities and desiring rather to surpass one another in them, and all of them being worthy of their leader and of the virtue that surrounded him.

One could see how deeply they loved Eleazar, being reluctant to be parted from him, and how he loved them; for besides having written to the king concerning their return, he repeatedly urged Andreas and me to take action, begging us to assist in whatever way we could.

And when we promised to give careful thought to these matters, he said he was still deeply anxious; for he knew that the king, being a lover of good men, considers it the greatest of all things to summon to himself, wherever someone may be celebrated, any person who surpasses others in conduct and wisdom.

For I have learned that he rightly says that, by keeping righteous and prudent men around himself, he would have the greatest protection for his kingdom, since his friends advise him with frankness for what is advantageous; and this quality indeed belongs to those being sent by him.
And he confirmed with oaths that he would not let the men go if any other private necessity pressed upon him, but was sending them out for the common benefit of all the citizens.

For living nobly consists in observing the laws, and this is accomplished through hearing far more than through reading. In setting forth these and similar statements, then, he made clear his affection toward them.

It is worth mentioning briefly what he explained in response to the questions we raised. For I think most people feel some curiosity regarding the regulations in the Law concerning meats and drinks and the animals considered to be unclean.

For when we inquired why, since there is a single creation, some things are considered unclean for eating, and some even for touching—for the Law seems scrupulous in most things, but in these matters exceedingly scrupulous—he began his reply as follows:

'You see,' he said, 'what an effect associations and companionships produce: by keeping company with the wicked, people acquire corruptions and become wretched throughout their entire lives; but if they live together with the wise and prudent, they obtain a reformation from ignorance for their life.

Our lawgiver, therefore, having first defined the matters of piety and justice, and having taught each detail concerning them, not only by prohibitions but also by positive instruction, making evident both the harms and the punishments sent by God upon the guilty—

for he demonstrated first of all that God is one, and that his power is made manifest through all things, every place being filled with his sovereignty, and that nothing done secretly by people on earth escapes him, but whatever anyone does is manifest to him, as well as things yet to come—

having elaborated these matters with precision and made them clear, he showed that even if someone merely intends to commit wickedness, he could not escape notice, let alone if he actually does it, demonstrating the power of God throughout the entire legislation.
Having made this beginning, and having shown that all other people besides us believe in many gods, though they are themselves far more powerful than the things they vainly worship—

for having made statues of stone and wood, they claim that these are images of those who discovered something useful for their livelihood, and they bow down before them, though having insensibility right beside their feet.

For if anyone should be a god on that account, by virtue of an invention, it is utterly senseless; for they merely took certain things found in creation, put them together, and showed them to be useful, without having made their substance themselves; therefore it is empty and futile to deify fellow humans.

Indeed, even now there are many people more inventive and more learned than those of earlier times, and people would never finish worshiping them! Yet those who fashioned and mythologized these things believe that they are the wisest of the Greeks.

For what need is there even to speak of the other utterly foolish peoples, the Egyptians and those like them, who have placed their reliance on wild beasts and most creeping things and reptiles, and worship these, and sacrifice to them both while alive and when dead?—

Our wise lawgiver, therefore, having observed each matter and having been equipped by God with understanding of all things, fenced us about with impenetrable palisades and iron walls, so that we should not mingle with any of the other nations in any way, remaining pure in body and in soul, set free from futile opinions, worshiping the only and almighty God above the whole creation.

For this reason, the leading priests among the Egyptians, who have looked deeply into many matters and are experienced in affairs, call us "people of God"—a title that does not belong to the rest of humanity, unless someone worships the true God, but they are rather people of food, drink, and shelter.

For their entire disposition is directed toward these things. But among our people, these things are accounted as nothing, while their reflection throughout their whole life is on the sovereignty of God.

Therefore, so that we might not be corrupted by associating with anyone or consorting with the base, he hedged us around on every side with purifications, through our food, drink, touches, hearing, and sight, in accordance with the Law.

For, on the whole, all things are constituted in harmony with natural reason, being governed by a single power, and each individual thing has a profound reason behind what we abstain from using and what we make use of. By way of example, I will touch briefly upon one or two points and explain them to you.

For do not fall into the degraded notion that Moses laid down these laws out of an anxious curiosity about mice and weasels or such things; rather, all things have been solemnly ordained for holy contemplation and the moral formation of character for the sake of righteousness.

For of the birds that we use, all are tame and distinguished by their cleanliness, feeding on wheat and pulses, such as doves, turtledoves, locusts, partridges, and further geese and all other such kinds.

But regarding the birds that are forbidden, you will find that they are wild and carnivorous, dominating the rest through their own strength and obtaining their food by unjustly preying upon the aforementioned tame birds; and not only these, but they also snatch away lambs and kids, and do harm to human beings, both dead and living.

By calling them unclean, he therefore set a symbolic mark through them, indicating that those for whom the legislation has been ordained ought in their soul to practice righteousness and not tyrannize over anyone, relying on their own strength, nor take anything away, but rather govern the affairs of life justly—just as the tame creatures among the aforementioned birds consume what grows from legumes upon the earth and do not tyrannize to the destruction of their own kind.
Through such things, then, the Lawgiver has handed down a sign to the discerning to be righteous and to accomplish nothing by violence, nor, relying on their own power, to oppress others.

For where it is not even fitting to touch the aforementioned creatures because of the disposition inherent in each, how must one not completely guard against allowing one's character to be corrupted in this way?

All the permissions granted to us regarding these creatures and the cattle have therefore been set forth figuratively. For the cloven hoof and the parting of the cleft of the claws is a symbol of distinguishing each of our actions toward what is good.

For the strength of whole bodies along with their activity rests upon the shoulders and the legs. The symbolism of these things therefore compels us to perform everything with distinction directed toward righteousness; and furthermore, because we have been set apart from all other human beings.

For most other people defile themselves through their intermingling, committing great iniquity, and whole regions and cities pride themselves on these things. For they not only consort with males, but even defile mothers and daughters. But we have been kept distinct from these things.

And alongside the aforementioned principle of distinction, he has also stamped the principle of memory. For all creatures that are cloven-hoofed and bring up the cud clearly convey the symbol of memory to those who understand.
For the chewing of the cud is nothing other than the recollection of life and existence, since he considers that life is sustained through food.

Therefore, in the Scripture, the one who speaks commands thus: "You shall surely remember the Lord who did great and wonderful things in you." For when contemplated, they appear both great and glorious: first, the construction of the body, the digestion of food, and the distinct function of each limb;

but much more so the arrangement of the senses, the operation of the mind and its invisible motion, as well as the agility in acting with respect to each thing and the invention of arts, which encompass an boundless manner of operation.

Therefore he commands us to keep in memory how the aforementioned things are preserved by divine power and design. For he has appointed every time and place for remembering always the God who rules and preserves.

For indeed, in the matter of food and drink, he commands us to partake only after offering firstfruits. Furthermore, he has given us a token of remembrance upon our garments, and likewise he has commanded us to place the divine words upon our gates and doors, in order that there may be a remembrance of God.

He also explicitly commands the sign to be bound around the hands, clearly demonstrating that every action must be performed with righteousness, keeping in mind our own creation, and above all, the fear of God.

He also commands us, both when going to rest and when rising up, to meditate upon the works of God, not only in word, but observing by mental apprehension our own motion and consciousness when going to sleep, and our waking up, how divine and incomprehensible is the transition between them.

Thus the excellence of the teaching regarding distinction and memory has been shown to you, as we explained the cloven hoof and the chewing of the cud. For these laws were not established at random or according to whatever entered the mind, but with a view to truth and the signification of right reason.
For having given instructions concerning food and drink and each matter of touch, he commands that we neither do nor hear anything heedlessly, nor turn to injustice by misusing the power of speech.
And the same principle is to be found in the case of the wild beasts; for the character of the weasel and of similar animals, all that are forbidden, is destructive.
For mice ruin and harm everything, not only for the sake of their own nourishment, but so as to render entirely useless to humans whatever they set out to harm.
And the species of the weasel is unique; for besides what has been said, it has a pernicious disposition: it conceives through the ears and gives birth through the mouth.

And for this reason, such a character in human beings is unclean; for those who, having received things through hearing, give them body in speech, have plunged others into misfortune and perpetrated no ordinary evil, having themselves become completely defiled with the pollution of impiety. And your king does well to execute such people, as we hear."

And I said, "I think you are speaking of the informants; for he continually subjects them to tortures and painful deaths." And he replied, "Indeed, it is these I mean; for watching intently for the destruction of people is unholy.

But our Law commands us to harm no one either by word or by deed. Concerning these matters, then, I have briefly gone through them, showing you in addition that all things have been regulated with a view to righteousness, and nothing has been prescribed in the Scripture haphazardly or mythologically, but so that throughout our whole life and in our actions we might practice righteousness toward all people, mindful of the sovereign God.
Every teaching concerning foods, therefore, and unclean reptiles and wild beasts, tends toward righteousness and righteous human interaction."

To me, then, he seemed to defend each point admirably. For regarding the calves, rams, and he-goats that are offered, he also said that one must take these tame animals from herds and flocks to sacrifice, and nothing wild, so that those offering the sacrifices might not be conscious of any arrogance in themselves, using the sign provided by the Lawgiver. For the one who brings the sacrifice makes an offering of the entire disposition of his own soul.

Concerning these matters, then, I consider the contents of his discourse worthy of recount; therefore, because of your love of learning, Philocrates, I have been prompted to explain to you the solemnity and natural meaning of the Law.
Eleazar, having offered sacrifice, selected the men, and prepared many gifts for the king, sent us on our way with great security.
When we arrived in Alexandria, the king was notified of our arrival. Andreas and I, having been admitted to the court, greeted the king warmly and delivered the letters from Eleazar.
Since he considered it of great importance to meet the men who had been sent, he ordered all the other officials in charge of affairs to be dismissed and the men to be summoned.

When this appeared extraordinary to everyone—because it was the custom that those who arrived on official business should come into the king's presence on the fifth day, while envoys from kings or prominent cities were admitted to the court with difficulty after thirty days—yet deeming those who had arrived worthy of greater honor and judging the preeminence of the sender, he dismissed those he considered superfluous and waited, walking about until he might greet them as they arrived.

When they entered with the gifts that had been sent and the exquisite parchments on which the Law had been written in gold in Jewish characters—the parchment having been wonderfully prepared, and the joining of the sheets made imperceptible—when the king saw the men, he asked about the scrolls.

And when they uncovered the wrappings and unrolled the membranes, after pausing for a long time and making obeisance about seven times, he said: “I give thanks to you, men, but still more to him who sent you, and most of all to God, whose oracles these are.”

And when all cried out with one accord in a single voice, both those who had arrived and those present: “Well spoken, O King!” he was moved to tears, filled with joy. For the tension of the soul and the excess of honor compel one to weep in times of success.

Having ordered the scrolls to be returned to their order, he then greeted the men and said: “It was right, godly men, first to pay reverence to those things for the sake of which I sent for you, and after that to extend my right hand to you; therefore I have done this first.”

“And I regard this day on which you have arrived as great, and it shall be distinguished every year throughout the whole time of our life; for it has also coincided with our receiving news of victory in the naval battle against Antigonus. Therefore I also desire to dine with you today.”

“Everything,” he said, “will be fittingly provided for you, which you will use, and for me with you.” When they expressed their pleasure, he commanded that the finest lodgings near the citadel be given to them, and that arrangements for the banquet be prepared.

The chief steward Nicanor, having summoned Dorotheus, who was appointed over these matters, commanded him to complete the preparation for each one. For it had been so arranged by the king, as you even now observe; for as many cities as there are that follow their own customs regarding food, drink, and bedding, there were as many appointed officials; and arrangements were made according to their customs whenever they came before the kings, so that experiencing no discomfort, they might pass their time pleasantly; which was indeed done for these men.

For Dorotheus, being a most attentive man, had the supervision of such matters. And he spread out all the furnishings under his care, which had been set apart for such receptions. And he made the seating arrangements in two sections, just as the king commanded; for he ordered half of them to recline beside his own hand, and the rest next to his own couch, neglecting nothing to honor the men.

And when they had reclined, he commanded Dorotheus to carry out the service according to the customs used by all who come to him from Judea. Therefore he excused the sacred heralds and sacrificers and the others whose custom it was to offer prayers; and he requested Eleazar, who was the senior priest among those who had come with us, to offer a prayer. He stood up and said memorably:

“May Almighty God fill you, O King, with all the good things he has created; and may he grant these to you, your wife, your children, and those of one mind with you, to possess them unfailingly for the whole duration of life!”

When he had said these things, applause broke out with shouting and joyful delight for a considerable time; and then they turned to enjoy the dishes that had been prepared, all the services being performed under the direction of Dorotheus; among the attendants were also royal pages and those honored by the king.

And when he found an opportunity after an interval, he asked the one who occupied the first seat (for they had taken their places according to age): “How might one continue to keep his kingdom unassailable to the end?”

After pausing for a moment, he said: “You would best direct it by imitating the constant clemency of God. For by practicing longsuffering and correcting those who deserve it more gently than they deserve, you will turn them from wickedness and lead them to repentance.”

The king praised him and asked the next: “How might one act well in every affair?” And he replied: “If one maintains justice toward all, one will act well in every affair for oneself, understanding that every thought is clear to God; and if you take the fear of God as your starting point, you would fail in nothing.”

And having warmly approved this man as well, he asked another: “How might one have friends like oneself?” And that one said: “If they see you taking great care for the multitudes over whom you rule; and you will do this by observing how God benefits the human race, providing them with health, food, and all other things in their proper season.”

Concurring with this man, he asked the next: “How might one gain praise in audiences and judicial decisions, even from those who fail to obtain their requests?” And he said: “If you are impartial in speech toward all, and do nothing haughtily or by your own power against those who err.”

“And you will do this by looking to the ordinance of God; for requests that are suitable are fulfilled for the worthy, while to those who fail to obtain them it is shown through dreams or deeds that their requests are harmful to them, God not striking them according to their sins nor according to the greatness of his power, but dealing with them in clemency.”

Having warmly praised this man too, he asked the next: “How might one be invincible in the demands of war?” And he said: “If one does not put confidence in multitudes or armed forces, but calls upon God through all things, that he may direct one's undertakings when conducting all affairs justly.”

And accepting this man also, he asked another: “How might one be fearsome to his enemies?” And he said: “If, while possessing an abundant preparation of arms and forces, one knows that these are futile over a longer time for achieving the outcome; for God also, by granting respite and showing the fear of his dominion, instills it in every mind.”

And having praised this man too, he said to the next: “What would be the most excellent thing for him in life?” And that one said: “To know that God rules over all, and that in our finest deeds we do not ourselves direct what has been planned, but God brings all things to completion and leads them, holding dominion.”

Having applauded him as well for speaking well, he asked another: “How might one, having preserved all things intact, pass on the same condition to his descendants in the end?” And he said: “By continually praying to God to receive good thoughts for the actions to be done, and by admonishing his descendants not to be overwhelmed by glory or wealth; for it is God who grants these things, and they do not have preeminence over all through themselves.”

Commending these words, he inquired of the next one: “How might one bear what happens with moderation?” And that one said: “If you realize in advance that all humans have been created by God to share in the greatest evils, and likewise in good things, and that it is impossible for a human being to be without a share in these; but God gives courage of heart, whom it is necessary to beseech.”

Having treated this man cordially too, he said that they had all spoken well: “And having questioned one more, I will stop for the present, so that we may turn to enjoyment and pass the time pleasantly. But during the six successive days after this, I will learn something more from the rest in turn.”

Then he asked the man: “What is the goal of courage?” And he said: “If what has been rightly deliberated is executed according to purpose in the actions of dangerous moments. And all things are brought to advantageous completion by God for you, O King, when you deliberate well.”

When all applauded and indicated their approval with clapping, the king said to the philosophers (for not a few of them were present with them): “I think these men excel in virtue and understand more, who on the spur of the moment have received such questions and answered as is fitting, all making God the beginning of their speech.”

And Menedemus, the philosopher of Eretria, said: “Yes, O King; for since the universe is governed by providence, and these men have rightly assumed that humankind is God's creation, it follows that all power and beauty of speech originate from God.”
When the king nodded assent, the discussion about these things ceased, and they turned to merriment. And when evening overtook them, the banquet came to an end.

On the next day, the arrangements for reclining and the banquet were carried out again in the same order. And when the king thought it was a suitable time to make an inquiry of the men, he questioned those next in order after those who had answered on the previous day.
He began to converse with the eleventh man, for ten had been questioned on the previous day. When silence was established, he inquired: “How might one remain wealthy?”

After pausing for a moment, the one receiving the question said: “If one does nothing unworthy of his rule or insolent, nor exhausts expenditure on vain and futile things, but leads his subjects to goodwill toward himself through beneficence; for God is the author of good things to all, whom it is necessary to follow.”

Having praised this man, the king asked another: “How might one preserve truth?” And he answered to this: “By knowing that falsehood brings great disgrace upon all humans, and much more upon kings; for since they have authority to do whatever they wish, for what reason should they lie? And you must understand this, O King: that God is a lover of truth.”

Having warmly approved this man too, he looked at him and said: “What is the teaching of wisdom?” And the other declared: “Just as you do not wish evil things to be present with yourself, but to be a partaker of all good things, so you should act toward your subjects and those who err, admonishing the noble and good among people more gently; for God also guides all humans with clemency.”

Having praised him, he said to the one after him: “How might one be philanthropic?” And that one said: “By observing how the human race is born and grows through much time and the greatest hardships; wherefore one ought neither to punish easily nor inflict mistreatment, knowing that human life consists in pains and penalties. Considering each of these things, you will turn toward mercy; for God is merciful.”

And accepting this man, he inquired of the next in order: “What is the most necessary manner of kingship?” “To keep oneself uncorrupted by gifts,” he said, “and to be sober the greater part of life, and to honor justice and make friends of those who are like-minded; for God is a lover of justice.”

Having applauded this man also, he said to the next, "What is the true state of piety?" And he said, "To recognize that God works and knows all things continually, and that no human being who commits an unjust deed or works evil could escape his notice; for just as God does good to the whole world, so you too, by imitating him, would be without offense."

Approving this answer, he said to the next, "What is the definition of kingship?" And he said, "To rule oneself well, and not to be carried away by wealth and glory to desire something arrogant and dishonorable, if you reason properly. For all things are present to you as nothing. But God is in need of nothing and is equitable. So you also, bear in mind that you are human, and do not reach after many things, but only what is sufficient for reigning as king."

Highly praising him, he asked the next, "How might one deliberate in the noblest way?" And he answered, "If one continually puts justice forward in everything and considers injustice to be the deprivation of life; for indeed God continually foreshadows the greatest goods for the righteous."

Having praised this man, he said to the next in order, "How might one be untroubled in sleep?" And he said, "You have asked a difficult question to answer. For in the events of sleep we cannot control ourselves, but are held by an irrational perception in these matters."

"For in our soul we experience things presented to us as if they were actually seen; and we are irrational to the extent that we imagine ourselves walking upon the sea and traveling in ships, or soaring through the air and crossing to other places, and other such things, yet he who imagines these things is not sound of mind."

"However, as far as it is within my grasp, I have reached this conclusion: you must in every way, O king, refer both your words and your actions to piety, so that you may be conscious in yourself that, preserving virtue, you do not choose to grant favors contrary to reason, nor do you use authority to set justice aside."

"For, for the most part, whatever matters occupy each person during waking hours, the mind also revolves around those same things in sleep; but one who directs every thought and deed toward the noblest ends guides them straight both awake and asleep. Wherefore in your case there is always tranquility."
Having applauded this man also, he said to the next, "Since you are the tenth to give an answer, as soon as you have spoken, we will turn to dinner."

And he asked, "How might we do nothing unworthy of ourselves?" And he said, "Look continually upon your own glory and preeminence, so that you may speak and think in accordance with these, knowing that all over whom you rule both think and speak about you."

"For you must not appear inferior to the actors; for considering the character that it is necessary for them to portray, they perform all things in accordance with it. But you are not acting a part; you are truly king, God having given you sovereign rule in a manner worthy of your character."

When the king had warmly applauded him with good will for some time, they invited the men to go to sleep. And when matters concerning them had ended, they turned to the next arrangement of the banquet.

On the following day, when the same arrangement had taken place and the king considered it to be the proper time to inquire something of the men, he asked the first of those remaining for the next question, "What is the best form of rule?"
And he said, "To rule oneself and not to be swept along by one's impulses. For it is natural for all human beings for their mind to incline toward something:

the majority are naturally inclined toward food, drink, and pleasures, but kings toward the acquisition of territory, in proportion to the greatness of their glory. Yet moderation in all things is noble. What God gives, take and hold fast; but do not desire what is unattainable."

Pleased with what was said, he said to the next, "How might one be free from envy?" Pausing a moment, he said, "First, if he understands that God distributes glory and great wealth to all kings, and no one is king by himself; for all wish to share in this glory, but cannot, since it is God's gift."

Having praised the man at length, he asked the next, "How might one despise his enemies?" And he said, "By practicing goodwill toward all people and forging friendships, you would take account of no one; and to have found favor with all people and to have received a noble gift from God—this is the best thing."

Agreeing with this, he commanded the next in order to reply, saying to him, "How might one continue to be held in glory?" And he said, "By being generous and magnificent in readiness and favors toward others, you will never lack glory; but so that what has been spoken of may abide with you, call upon God continually."

Applauding this man, he asked another, "How ought one to show generous ambition?" And he said, "Toward those who are friendly to us, everyone thinks it is necessary to show it; but I consider that one ought to display a gracious ambition toward opponents, so that in this way we may bring them over to what is proper and beneficial to themselves. But one must entreat God that these things may be accomplished, for he rules the minds of all."

Concurring with this, he commanded the sixth to declare his view, asking, "To whom ought one to show favor?" And he answered, "To parents continually, for God also has given a great commandment concerning the honor of parents. And next in order he approves the relationship with friends, having called a friend equal to one's own soul. But you do well in establishing all people in friendship toward yourself."

Encouraging this man also, he inquired of the next, "What is worthy of beauty?" And he said, "Piety; for this is indeed a preeminent kind of beauty. Its power is love, for this is God's gift; and you also possess this, embracing in it all good things."

Having applauded very cordially, he said to another, "How might one who has stumbled regain the same glory?" And he said, "For you it is impossible to stumble, for you have sown seeds of favor among all, which produce goodwill; and goodwill, prevailing over the greatest weapons, encompasses the greatest security.

But if any do stumble, they must no longer do those things on account of which they stumbled, but having acquired friendship, they must practice justice. It is God's gift to be a worker of good things and not of their opposites."

Being pleased with these words, he said to the next, "How might one be free from grief?" And he said, "If one harms no one, but benefits all, following justice; for the fruits born of it produce freedom from grief.

One must also entreat God that things arising contrary to our intention may not harm us—I mean such things as deaths, diseases, pains, and the like. But since you are pious, none of these things would come upon you."

Having praised this man handsomely, he asked the tenth, "What is the highest degree of glory?" And he said, "To honor God; and this is done not with gifts or sacrifices, but with purity of soul and holy conviction, recognizing that all things are framed and governed by God according to his will. You continually maintain this disposition, as everyone can observe from what you have accomplished and are accomplishing."

In a louder voice the king greeted them all and encouraged them, while those present cheered in assent, especially the philosophers. For indeed they far surpassed them in conduct and speech, inasmuch as they made their beginning from God. After this, the king proceeded to display his hospitality by proposing toasts.

On the following day, when the arrangement of the banquet was conducted in the same manner, as soon as an opportune moment came for the king, he questioned those next in order after those who had already answered, saying to the first, "Can wisdom be taught?" And he said, "It is a disposition of the soul through divine power to receive all that is noble and to turn away from the contrary."
Agreeing, he asked the next, "What contributes most to health?" And he said, "Self-control; but it is not possible to attain this unless God disposes the mind toward it."
